title: Course Introduction
text:
Welcome to Math 393
Welcome to Math 393 Abstract Algebra! I am Prof. Geoffrey Buhl, and I am you instructor for this semester. Buhl rhymes with fuel.
Class Session Goals:

Meet Classmates and work in small groups.
Learn about this course and my expectations.
Work on a first discrete mathematics problem.

title: Course Introduction
text:
Syllabus Activity

Take a few minutes to introduce yourselves and share what other courses you are taking this semester.
As a group, take 10–15 minutes to look over the syllabus and formulate four questions your group would like to ask about the course.
As a whole class, groups will ask questions and I will answer them.

title: Course Introduction
text:
Advice for students

Start homework early, do it consistently, and redo missed or difficult problems since homework closely matches exam questions.
Attend every lecture, pay attention, take clear notes, and ask questions to fully understand concepts and proofs.

title: Course Introduction
section: How I will teach this course
text:
How I will teach this course
I cannot cover everything in the text or in a given chapter or section. I will focus on the most important concepts and proofs, and I will provide additional examples and exercises to help you understand the material. I will also provide additional resources and references for further study. Ask questions in class, during office hours, or via email. Part of you preparation for the class is to read the text beforehand.

title: Course Introduction
text:
Activity 1
Take a few moments to introduce yourselves to your group members.
Then in small groups, work write out all the rotations of the square and pentagon. Then create a composition table for the rotations of the square and pentagon.

title: Course Introduction
text:
Activity 2
Take a few moments to introduce yourselves to your group members.
Now we will allow flips or reflections of the triangle and square. What are the addtional symmetries of the triangle and square? Then create a composition table for the symmetries of the triangle and square that includes both rotations and reflections.

title: Course Introduction
text:
Activity 3
Take a few moments to introduce yourselves to your group members.
What about a tetrahedron? You can rotate around a face/vertex or edge or vertex. List out the symmetries of the tetrahedron. Then create a composition table for the symmetries of the tetrahedron.
What about a cube? You can rotate around a face, edge or vertex. List out the symmetries of the cube. Then create a composition table for the symmetries of the cube.
we’ll just label the faces of these objects because that is how the dice are labeled.

title: Equivalence Relations and Division Algorithm
text:
Class Session Goals

Learn about Equivalence Relations and see examples
Practice determining whether a relation is an equivalence relation
Prove the Division Algorithm

title: Equivalence Relations
text:
1.13. Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(\mathbb{N}\) via \(a \sim b\) if and only if \(a-b=3k\), for some \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\). Is \(\sim\) an equivalence relation? If so, what are the equivalence classes?
1.14. Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}\) via \(a \sim b\) if and only if \(a\) and \(b\) are both even or both odd. Is \(\sim\) an equivalence relation? If so, what are the equivalence classes?
1.15. Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(\mathbb{Z}\) via \(a \sim b\) if and only if \(|a|=|b|\). Is \(\sim\) an equivalence relation? If so, what are the equivalence classes?
1.16. Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(\mathbb{Z}\) via \(a \sim b\) if and only if \(ab>0\). Is \(\sim\) an equivalence relation? If so, what are the equivalence classes?
1.17. Let \(S\) be the set of all subsets of \(\mathbb{Z}\). Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(S\) via \(T \sim U\) if and only if \(T \subseteq U\). Is \(\sim\) an equivalence relation? If so, what are the equivalence classes?
1.18. Let \(S\) be the set of all subsets of \(\mathbb{Z}\). Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(S\) via \(T \sim U\) if and only if \(T \setminus U\) and \(U \setminus T\) are both finite. Show that \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation and describe \([\{1,2,3\}]\) and \([\{\ldots,-4,-2,0,2,4,\ldots\}]\).
25. Determine whether or not the following relations are equivalence relations on the given set. If the relation is an equivalence relation, describe the partition given by it. If the relation is not an equivalence relation, state why it fails to be one.

\(x \sim y\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) if \(x \ge y\)
\(m \sim n\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\) if \(mn>0\)
\(x \sim y\) in \(\mathbb{R}\) if \(|x-y| \le 4\)
\(m \sim n\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\) if \(m \equiv n \pmod{6}\)

title: Math 393 Syllabus
text:
Professor: Geoffrey Buhl
Email: geoffrey.buhl@csuci.edu
Phone: 805-437-3122
Office: 2324 Marin Hall
Office hours: MW 9:00–10:00am or by appointment
Course meetings: Monday and Wednesday, 10:30–11:45am
Course textbook: Abstract Algebra: Theory and Applications, Thomas W. Judson
Course website: CI Learn




Groups, rings, and fields! Oh My! These are the core algebraic structures in mathematics. Finally we get to the good stuff: axiomatic mathematics and discussing the rules and structures that are the baseline tools for all of mathematics. Groups describe symmetry and have rich and interesting structure that arise from 3 simple axioms.



Prerequisite: MATH 240 and MATH 310
Groups, rings, and fields, the basic algebraic structures in contemporary mathematics.



The best way to get in touch with me is in-person or by email. In general, if you have any difficulties with the material, schedule, or anything else, get in touch with me. I’m here to help, and it’s much easier to help if you are proactive. If my office hours don’t work for you, email me and we can work out a time to me in-person or via Zoom.




Discuss the basic algebraic structures appearing in mathematics today
Apply the knowledge of these structures to the analysis of concrete special cases
Compute degrees of extensions
Prove impossibility of certain ruler and compass geometric constructions, e.g. squaring of the circle
Parametrize field extensions by groups and vice-versa
Determine the solvability of higher degree polynomial equations by radicals
Express concepts and techniques of Abstract Algebra in oral and written form

Group work, collaborations, and the free exchange of ideas are fundamental aspects of an academic environment. I encourage you all to talk and work with others in the class, as it will enhance your understanding of the material. You must write up your assignment individually and explain solutions in your own words. It is also important to cite resources you used in work, these may include other students, books, websites, and instructors.
There is a distinction between collaboration and copying. Collaboration is encouraged; copying solutions or assignments is not allowed. If I find copying of solutions on an assignment it will result in a score of 0 on that assignment. Multiple instances of academic dishonesty will be formally documented with the University.
Academic Honesty and Generative AI: I have begun to notice students submitting work generated by AI. This is copying. If I suspect AI has been used on an assignment, I will assign a score of 0, but you can present your work in office hours or by appointment to receive credit.
